Read Hero’s Greek

Hero, Pneumatics I.42, Schmidt (1899), p. 192:

ἐν δὲ τῷ ὕδατι κοῖλον ἡμισφαίριον κατεστραμμένον ἔστω

In the water let there be a hollow hemisphere, turned upside down.

New English translation. The transcription rejoins a printed word across lines and removes an older-page marker within κοῖλον.

ἐν δὲ τῷ ὕδατι

en de tōi hydati — In the water. Here ἐν takes the dative for location; τῷ and ὕδατι are dative singular. The headword ὕδωρ changes its stem to ὑδατ- in this form. δέ connects the new instruction to the previous one.

κοῖλον

koilon — Hollow. A neuter singular adjective agreeing with ἡμισφαίριον. A solid half-ball would not hold the air pocket shown in the experiment. The identical neuter nominative and accusative forms are distinguished here by the sentence's construction.

ἡμισφαίριον

hēmisphairion — Hemisphere. A neuter singular noun, the subject of ἔστω. The beginning ἡμι- means half; compare English hemisphere. It tells us a form, but gives no radius, wall thickness or exact water fill.

κατεστραμμένον

katestrammenon — Turned upside down. A perfect middle/passive participle of καταστρέφω, here describing the resulting inverted state. Its neuter singular ending agrees with ἡμισφαίριον, just as κοῖλον does. The printed word continues across two lines.

ἔστω

estō — Let there be. Third-person singular present imperative of εἰμί, to be. Technical Greek often sets up an object this way. The instruction gives us a hollow hemisphere in an inverted position.

Vitruvius’s “inverted funnel” need not mean a cone: Roman funnels could be rounded. Hagel (2023, pp. 55–60) discusses the two descriptions together. The cone in this study is a mathematical comparison. Read the research paper.

The calculation

Water conserved. Air accounted for.

The full chamber starts with inside water at its open rim. Withdrawing air lets that surface rise and the outside surface fall. The vertical difference supports the pressure. The comparison holds the rim radius, chamber height, tank plan and initial fill fixed; the three chambers have different volumes and full pressures.

Read the equations and limits

Heights are measured above the open rim. Let T be the tank area, F(z) the chamber volume below height z, and z₀ the initial water level before pumping. With negligible wall thickness:

T × outside − F(outside) + F(inside) = T × z₀
head = outside − inside
gauge pressure = 1000 × 9.80665 × head
ambient gas stock = actual air volume × (1 + gauge pressure / 101325)

Volume integrals and monotone bisection solve the two water levels. Gas supplied is the decrease in ambient-equivalent stock. The separate decrease in actual volume is a geometric quantity; compression makes them differ.

The model is isothermal and static. It omits waves, metal thickness, neck and windchest volume, leakage, under-rim clearance, time and pipe acoustics. A high-filled chamber can empty while its last pocket still has a positive limiting head; an empty chamber supplies no wind. The selected pressure drop is a criterion for this experiment, not an ancient performance specification.

Hagel’s 80 cm hemisphere example gives about 134 L full volume and 653 mm head. Its roughly 50 L geometric release for a 30% pressure drop becomes about 54.72 ambient-equivalent L under this model’s isothermal correction. His paper labels the geometric treatment’s omission of compression (p. 65, note 21). These are reconstruction calculations, not measured ancient operating values.
